newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition, SPD set to jump start tax talks.
newsitem.headline: German coalition, SPD set to jump start tax talks.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) proclaimed their readiness over the weekend to jump-start stalled talks on a sweeping overhaul of Germany's tax system.

High profile negotiations on Germany's future tax structure collapsed last weekend after the SPD withdrew to protest against cuts in coal industry subsidies, but an end to that dispute on Thursday has cleared the way for a new "tax summit."
"If the SPD is serious, we could have the cornerstone of an agreement within 14 days," Finance Minister Theo Waigel told the Bild newspaper's Saturday edition.
SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said that while the two sides were far apart, an agreement had to be reached to spur the German economy and reduce record high unemployment.
"I am ready to meet with the Chancellor," Lafontaine told Der Spiegel magazine. "But we must reach a decision that will really help in the war against unemployment."
At issue are legislative proposals put forward by Waigel on Friday designed to to boost the economy and create jobs through supply-side policies of cutting income and corporate taxes.
The tax plan, worth up to 30 billion marks in net cuts, would broaden the tax base and simplify Germany's tax system.

The bulk of the tax reform, however, would not take effect until 1999, too late to give Bonn a substantial lift in its uphill fight to qualify for European economic and monetary union whose membership will be decided early next year.

Although the SPD shares the government's desire to stimulate the economy by easing the tax burden, it has bitterly opposed aspects of the plan such as a lower top tax rate which, the SPD claims, will most benefit the rich.
Lafontaine said the key to any tax plan would be a "noticeable" cut in the tax burden for families and workers from January 1, 1998.
The leadership of the both the government and opposition are keen to hammer out a tax reform deal.

For Kohl, a "tax summit" agreement now could mean saving the package from possible defeat in the upper house, where the SPD have a majority. For Lafontaine, it could mean an opportunity to boost his image against that of the Chancellor.
But over the weekend, it was the ruling coalition who appeared to show the greatest willingness to compromise.

Waigel told the Bild newspaper he was willing to negotiate over his plans to tax work done on holidays and a night-work premium -- a proposal which the SPD had flatly rejected. Other leading members of the coalition pushed for the negotations to quickly start and expressed hope that an agreement may be within reach.

The chairman of the lower house of Parliament's finance committee, Carl-Ludwig Thiele, in an interview with the Bild am Sonntag newspaper, called on the SPD to "urgently return to the bargaining table in the coming week" and expressed a willingness to compromise on contentious issues.

The parliamentary leader of the Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), Hermann Otto Solms, told the Magdeburger Volksstimme newspaper if both side showed good will an agreement could be hammered out by Easter.
